# Slowness is not a bug

Jan Burzlaff1

Received: 1 April 2026 / Accepted: 21 April 2026 / Published online: 20 May 2026 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag London Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2026

Dear Editor:

In 1943, in a forest in southeastern Poland, a father walked his eleven-year-old daughter to the treeline and said: Do not turn back. She did not. Her parents were killed three months before liberation. Forty-five years later, Edith K. recounted this in a video testimony for the Fortunoff Archive at Yale. Last week I fed that testimony into ChatGPT. The model produced competent output. It identified themes of survival, false identity, and family separation. It tracked chronology and named locations. Asked about the moment at the forest’s edge, it reached for parental sacrifice, the weight of separation, a father’s impossible love. It was probabilistically apt and emotionally coherent. The model processed the words, but it did not register what it cost to say them, or to receive them, and then pass them on without smoothing over what they meant. This is not a complaint about accuracy. It is a complaint about evidence itself—about what AI does to specific records, not only to ideology at scale—and it is more structural, and more dangerous, than the familiar objections. AI systems are designed to resolve. They treat gaps as errors, ambiguity as something to be clarified away, silence as a problem awaiting solution—in testimony, and in any form of evidence where meaning resides as much in what is not said as in what is. When a student in my AI seminar asked ChatGPT to analyze a Danish survivor’s recollection of keeping a packed suitcase by her bed throughout the war, the model responded confidently: the suitcase reveals the emotional weight of constant fear and displacement. There was one problem. In the actual testimony, the survivor says the opposite. The suitcase was not emotionally difficult. It was simply an order from her parents. It was routine, yet AI could not accept this. The packed suitcase should carry emotional weight. So the model invented an affect the survivor

explicitly denied. One student put it precisely: “AI was just trying to give me something rather than giving a good analysis.” This is AI doing exactly what it is designed to do: completing the expected pattern, filling the gap with what is most probable. As Emily Bender and her colleagues argued in their widely discussed paper on “stochastic parrots” in 2021, these systems generate plausible language by statistical patterning rather than understanding. The difficulty in testimony analysis is not that the parrot squawks incorrectly—it is that it squawks fluently, and fluency forecloses the difficulty it was supposed to mediate. AI does not say “I cannot see this.” It fabricates plausible readings from contextual probability—what should be felt, given the events being described—rather than from what the evidence actually offers. A recent piece in this journal by Farhang Erfani argued that AI formats contingency as necessity, presenting its assumptions as procedural neutrality. My case is narrower but sharper: where Erfani maps what AI does to ideological meaning at scale, the testimony classroom reveals what it does to specific evidence—it completes what should remain incomplete, and in doing so produces not a distortion of the record but something worse, a record that sounds authoritative because it is fluent. The ideological and the evidential failures are the same operation at different scales. Naming the evidential register is what allows us to contest it with precision. The alternative is not to refuse AI but to be precise about what the human analyst must carry that AI cannot. In my seminar, students learn to read testimony for what resists resolution: the pause before an answer, the detail that contradicts the emotional logic of the narrative, the moment where a survivor says something that should not make sense and does. This is not passive reception but an active discipline of attention—noticing where language strains, where memory hedges, where the record is not incomplete but deliberately, meaningfully, stopped. The analyst who outsources that attention to a system optimized for pattern-completion does not save time. They lose the object.

Humanities disciplines have a name for what AI cannot do, even if we have not always used it explicitly. We can call it epistemic slowness: the willingness to sit with difficulty, to refuse premature resolution, and to hold open what should not be closed. This is not a preference: it is what makes interpretation possible at all—because without it, the object is replaced before it can be understood. It is not a luxury available only to tenured scholars at research universities. The International Council of Museums, in its 2022 redefinition, gestures towards exactly this disposition: museums are defined by their responsibility to communities, the public, and to what they hold in trust. Slowness here is not a pace, but a commitment—the refusal to treat the incomplete provenance as a problem, the unresolved testimony as noise awaiting signal. What AI threatens is not the pace of scholarly work but that commitment itself—replacing professional judgment with systems optimized for throughput and scale. Speed, then, is not a neutral value. When AI optimizes for resolution, it makes a methodological choice about what counts as evidence. It can hold a full transcript in view, flag patterns across hours of speech, perform linguistic labor that is genuinely useful. But the moment you ask it to interpret memory as testimony—something shaped as much by what cannot be said as by what is said—it fills gaps it cannot acknowledge and resolves what should remain open. That is not a bug. Resolution is the product. And slowness is the cost it will not pay. The risk is not the error you can catch but the interpretation that sounds authoritative because it is fluent and goes

unquestioned because fluency reads as care. The question is not how to use AI more effectively. It is how to name and defend a different relationship to evidence—one that treats the fragment not as incomplete data awaiting reconstruction, but as a finished record of what cannot be recovered. Do not turn back. A child walked out of the forest. Fortyfive years later, she spoke. That is not raw material but the very record. The work of the humanities is to receive it at full weight—which means resisting every system trained to make the weight disappear.
